title: What is known about 1RB0LE_1RC1RA_1RD0RF_1RE0RA_1LA1LD_1RA---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LE_1RC1RA_1RD0RF_1RE0RA_1LA1LD_1RA---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. The head sweeps across the whole tape. Read at the left end, the tape is a long list of numbers, each written as a run of the word 1 0 0; the sweeps count the first number down while the list grows at its other end, so the machine behaves like a queue of counters. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves the exact way a halt would happen (A>0 0 1 1) and how the sweeps cross the counters; the C simulator finds no halt in the first 1011 steps. The rule that produces new counters at the end of the list has not been worked out.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: How a halt comes about
claims.text: F reading 1 is the only halt. F is entered only from C reading 1, C only from B reading 0 and B only from A reading 0, all moving right (enter_F, enter_C, enter_B). So a halt is exactly C>1 1, that is B>0 1 1, that is A>0 0 1 1.

claims.title: Crossing the counters
claims.text: For every n and every surrounding tape, moving right: A turns (0 0 1 0 0 1)^n into (1 1 0 1 1 1)^n, F turns it into (1 1 1 1 1 0)^n, C turns (1 0 0 1 0 0)^n into (0 1 1 1 1 1)^n and B into (1 1 1 0 1 1)^n, each in twelve steps a block. Also A fills (0 1)^n and B fills (1 0)^n moving right, and E and A cross (0 1)^n and (1 0)^n moving left.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>11</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator (tools/c/tm.h) runs 1011 steps from blank tape without a halt; the visited tape then spans 811,363 cells, 404,207 of them 1.

claims.title: What A sees when it reads 0
claims.text: In the first 2·109 steps A reads 0 about 226 million times; the three cells after it are 0 1 0 or 1 0 0 in 96% of cases and otherwise 0 0 1, 0 0 0 or 1 0 1, never the halting 0 1 1.

claims.title: A queue of counters
claims.text: Each time the head reaches a fresh cell at the left end, the tape is a list of runs of 1s spaced three cells apart (the words 1 0 0 or 0 0 1), the runs separated by 0 0 0 0; read as numbers, for example 48, 17, 53, 7, 47, 15, 37, ... From one sweep to the next only the first number changes (it goes down by 2) and the last five or so numbers are rewritten in no visible pattern; when the first number runs out, the next one takes its place. The list grew to over 200 numbers in the first 5·107 steps, with occasional reorganisations that halve it.

claims.title: Growth shape
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.517). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.5).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. A proof would describe the queue: how a sweep pair acts on the first counter and on the end of the list, which new counters it appends, and why that never produces A>0 0 1 1. Queue-like machines of this kind can behave like tag systems, which are hard in general. Window CTL up to 7 cells and n-gram CPS (widths up to 9, see the README for the larger runs) fail.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. Started on a blank tape, this machine has run 10<sup>11</sup> steps without stopping. Read at the left end, its tape is a long list of numbers, and the sweeps of its head count the first number down while the list changes at the far end, like a queue. This page runs the real machine in your browser and shows the one pattern that would make it stop.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator.
Reached through B and C, all moving right.
The sweeps cross the counters, for any length.

sections.heading: A list of numbers
html: Stop the simulator each time the head reaches a fresh cell at the left end. The tape is made of 1s spaced three cells apart, in runs separated by one extra 0:

Read as a list, this is 48, 17, 53, 7, 47, 15, 37, ... From one such moment to the next only the first number changes (it goes down by 2) and the far end of the list is rewritten. When the first number is used up the next one takes its place. Every so often the list is reorganised (it went from 176 numbers to 88 at about 2.5·107 steps), and otherwise it grows.

sections.heading: Crossing the counters
html: Moving right, each state that crosses a counter rewrites it two words at a time (lean/Rules.lean, any length):

On the way back the blocks are turned into the spaced-out form again. Between the counters the separators 0 0 0 0 make the head turn into a different state, and that is where each counter gets changed.

sections.heading: The one way to halt
html: The only missing transition is F reading 1. F is entered only from C reading 1, C only from B reading 0, and B only from A reading 0, each step moving right. So the machine stops exactly when
This is proved in Lean (lean/Halt.lean). In 226 million visits the three cells after A's 0 were never 0 1 1.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.517). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.5).
After 109 steps the tape spans 73,887 cells (7,725 left of the start, 45,389 right), with a density of 1s of 0.594.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machines below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in any of the others, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: Bouncer whose tape is a long list of counters (runs of a 3-cell word, separated by an extra 0); each sweep eats into the first counter and the far end of the list changes, like a queue; it halts only at A>0 0 1 1.
family: two-sided bouncer, a queue of counters in the word 100
